topics.title: Operating System Roles & Dual-Mode Operations
topics.explanation:
• Operating System (OS): Acts as an intermediary bridge between computer hardware and user software programs. Kernal is the core of the operating system.
• Dual-Mode Operation: Uses a hardware mode bit to separate execution into User Mode (mode bit = 1) and Kernel Mode (mode bit = 0) to protect system resources.
• System Calls: Software interrupts/traps triggered when user programs request OS services like file access or process creation.
• Storage Hierarchy & DMA: Fast volatile storage (registers, cache, RAM) vs slower non-volatile storage (SSD, HDD). Direct Memory Access (DMA) transfers high-speed I/O blocks straight to RAM without constant CPU intervention.
topics.tldr: OS হলো Hardware এবং Software-এর bridge। Safe execution-এর জন্য CPU দুইটা mode ব্যবহার করে: User Mode (restricted) এবং Kernel Mode (privileged)।
keyPoints: Hardware interrupts come from devices; software traps come from errors or system call requests.
Base and limit registers ensure a user process cannot access memory outside its own boundary.
DMA generates only one interrupt per block of transferred data instead of one per byte.
examples: User Mode to Kernel Mode: Calling printf() in C internally triggers a write() system call to print to screen.
Privileged Instructions: Changing timer counters, managing page tables, and disabling interrupts.

traps.statement: Can user programs run privileged hardware instructions directly?
traps.explanation: No. User programs must make a system call to switch the CPU to Kernel Mode (mode bit 0) first.

topics.title: Process Memory Structure & Lifecycle
topics.explanation:
• Process: A program in active execution with its own dedicated memory space.
• Memory Layout: Composed of Text (code instructions), Data (global/static variables), Heap (dynamically allocated memory at runtime), and Stack (function arguments, local variables, return addresses).
• Process Control Block (PCB): The kernel data structure storing process state, program counter (PC), CPU registers, memory limits, and open file lists.
• States: New (creation) → Ready (waiting for CPU) → Running (executing) → Waiting/Blocked (waiting for I/O) → Terminated (finished).
topics.tldr: Program হলো passive file, আর Process হলো active execution। Process-এর memory-তে ৪টি part থাকে: Text, Data, Heap (dynamic) এবং Stack (local)।
keyPoints: Ready state means process is purely waiting for CPU allocation.
Waiting/Blocked state means process is waiting for external I/O or an event.
Context Switch: Pure overhead where CPU saves current PCB and restores another PCB.
examples: fork() creates a duplicate child process with pid = 0 returned to child and child PID returned to parent.
exec() replaces the process memory space with a completely new executable binary.

traps.statement: Are Ready and Waiting states the same?
traps.explanation: No. A ready process has all resources and only needs the CPU. A waiting process is stuck waiting for an I/O event.

topics.title: Threads, Multithreading Models & Amdahl's Law
topics.explanation:
• Thread: The smallest unit of execution inside a process; often called a lightweight process.
• Thread Resources: Threads in the same process share Code, Data, Heap, and open files, but maintain their own private Stack, Registers, and Program Counter.
• Multithreading Models: Many-to-One (user threads mapped to 1 kernel thread; blocking blocks all), One-to-One (each user thread gets 1 kernel thread; used in Linux/Windows), Many-to-Many.
• Amdahl's Law: Calculates the theoretical speedup limit of adding processor cores based on the serial portion of the program.
topics.tldr: Process আলাদা memory নেয়, কিন্তু একই process-এর Thread-রা Heap ও Code share করে শুধু নিজস্ব Stack ও Registers রাখে।
keyPoints: Thread creation and context switching are much faster and cheaper than process creation.
Concurrency means multiple tasks make progress; Parallelism means multiple tasks run simultaneously on multi-cores.
Amdahl's formula: Speedup <= 1 / (S + (1 - S) / N), where S is serial fraction and N is core count.

comparisons.title: Process vs Thread
rows: One crash does not affect others
One thread crash can kill whole process

traps.statement: Does multithreading always mean true parallel execution?
traps.explanation: No. On a single-core CPU, multithreading is concurrent time-slicing, not true hardware parallelism.

topics.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms & Criteria
topics.explanation:
• Optimization Goals: Keep the CPU busy, complete tasks quickly, and reduce waiting, turnaround, and response time.
• FCFS(First-Come,First-Serve): First process runs first; short jobs may wait behind long jobs (Convoy Effect).
• SJF(Shortest-Job-First): Shortest job runs first; SJF is non-preemptive, SRTF is preemptive.
• Round Robin: Each process gets a fixed time quantum; too large acts like FCFS, too small causes overhead.
• Priority Scheduling: Highest priority runs first; Starvation is solved using Aging.
topics.tldr: SJF সবচেয়ে কম average waiting time দেয়। Round Robin সবাইকে fair time slice (quantum) দেয়। Starvation ঠেকাতে Aging ব্যবহার হয়।
keyPoints: Turnaround Time = Completion Time - Arrival Time.
Waiting Time = Turnaround Time - Burst Time.
Multilevel Feedback Queue: Allows processes to move between queues based on CPU burst history.

comparisons.title: Scheduling Algorithms Comparison
rows: High context switch overhead if q is small

traps.statement: Should the Round Robin time quantum be extremely small?
traps.explanation: No. If too small, the CPU spends more time switching contexts than running actual instructions.

topics.title: Race Conditions, Critical Section & Semaphores
topics.explanation:
• Race Condition: Happens when multiple threads access shared data at the same time, causing different results based on execution order.
• Critical Section: A part of code that accesses shared data. It must ensure Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting.
• Mutex Lock: Allows only one thread at a time to enter the critical section.
• Semaphore: A variable used to control access to shared resources using wait() and signal(). Counting semaphores manage multiple resources, while binary semaphores work like mutexes.
topics.tldr: একই data একসাথে edit করলে Race Condition হয়। এটা থামাতে Mutex (1 জন access) বা Semaphore (N জন access) ব্যবহার করা হয়।
keyPoints: Peterson's algorithm is an algorithmic solution for 2 processes but fails on modern hardware due to instruction reordering.
Hardware instructions like Test-and-Set and Compare-and-Swap execute atomically to build robust locks.
Blocking semaphores put waiting processes onto a sleep queue to eliminate busy waiting.

traps.statement: Can any thread release a Mutex lock?
traps.explanation: No. A mutex must be unlocked by the exact thread that acquired it. A semaphore can be signaled by different threads.

topics.title: Deadlock Characterization, Prevention & Banker's Algorithm
topics.explanation:
• Deadlock: A state where two or more processes are permanently stuck because each holds a resource the other needs.
• 4 Coffman Conditions: Deadlock happens only if all 4 hold simultaneously. 
->1. Mutual Exclusion, 
->2. Hold and Wait, 
->3. No Preemption, 
->4. Circular Wait.
• Deadlock Prevention: Break at least one Coffman condition (e.g., impose strict global resource ordering to eliminate Circular Wait).
• Deadlock Avoidance (Banker's Algorithm): The OS grants resource requests only if the resulting state remains in a Safe State where at least one valid execution sequence exists without deadlock.
topics.tldr: Deadlock হতে হলে Coffman-এর ৪টি শর্ত একসাথে মিলতে হবে। যেকোনো ১টি শর্ত ভেঙে দিলে Deadlock কোনোদিন সম্ভব না।
keyPoints: Resource Allocation Graph (RAG): A cycle with single-instance resources confirms a deadlock; with multi-instances it only indicates possible deadlock.
Banker's Algorithm formula: Need matrix = Max claim - Current Allocation.
Deadlock Recovery strategies: Process termination (aborting cycles) or resource preemption with rollback.

comparisons.title: Deadlock Strategies
rows: Restricts resource requests to break 1 of 4 rules
Requires declaring max needs in advance
Allows deadlocks to happen, detects cycle, aborts

traps.statement: Does a cycle in a Resource Allocation Graph always mean a deadlock?
traps.explanation: Only if every resource has a single instance. If resources have multiple instances, a cycle does not guarantee deadlock.

topics.title: Virtual Memory, Paging, Page Faults & Thrashing
topics.explanation:
• Address: Think of it as a house address for data. The CPU uses a virtual address, and the MMU(Memory Management Unit) finds the real location in RAM.
• Paging: Memory is divided into small equal-sized blocks called Pages and Frames, making memory easier to manage.
• Page Table: Like a map that tells the system where each Page is located in RAM.
• Page Fault: Happens when the data is not currently in RAM, so the system must bring it from the disk.
• Thrashing: Happens when the computer spends too much time moving data between RAM and disk, making it very slow.
topics.tldr: Virtual Memory বড় program-কে ছোট RAM-এ চালায়। Page RAM-এ না থাকলে Page Fault হয়। RAM একদম কমে গেলে Thrashing হয়।
keyPoints: Internal fragmentation still occurs inside the final allocated page of a process.
Page faults are normal virtual memory events handled by the OS, not software bugs.
Thrashing is resolved by reducing the degree of multiprogramming or adding more physical RAM.

traps.statement: Is a Page Fault an application crash error?
traps.explanation: No. It is a standard hardware-OS mechanism to fetch missing pages on demand from disk into RAM.

topics.title: Scalability, Load Balancing & High Availability
topics.explanation:
• System Design: Planning system architecture, components, data flows, and infrastructure to meet traffic and business goals.
• Vertical Scaling (Scale Up): Adding more CPU, RAM, or storage to a single server; simple but hits hardware limits and single point of failure (SPOF).
• Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out): Adding more independent server instances; highly resilient, requires a load balancer.
• Load Balancer: Distributes network traffic across servers using algorithms like Round Robin, Least Connections, or IP Hash.
• Reliability vs Availability: Reliability measures correct continuous operation without bugs; Availability measures the percentage of time system remains reachable (e.g., 99.9% uptime).
topics.tldr: Scale Up মানে ১টা server বড় করা, Scale Out মানে অনেকগুলো server যোগ করা। Load Balancer সবার মধ্যে request ভাগ করে দেয়।
keyPoints: Single Point of Failure (SPOF): Any single component whose failure takes down the entire system.
High availability relies on redundancy, health checks, data replication, and automatic failovers.

traps.statement: Does putting a Load Balancer in front solve every scalability bottleneck?
traps.explanation: No. Unoptimized databases, slow disk I/O, and un-cached backend bottlenecks can still bring the system down.

topics.title: Common Technical Interview Questions
topics.explanation: High-yield interview questions focusing on operating systems and fundamental distributed architecture.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a Process and a Thread?
questions.answer: A process is an isolated executing program with its own memory space. A thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process that shares the process heap and code space.

questions.question: Why is Context Switching pure system overhead?
questions.answer: Because while saving registers, updating the PCB, and flushing CPU caches, no user application instructions are being computed.

questions.question: What are the four Coffman conditions necessary for a Deadlock?
questions.answer: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. All four must exist simultaneously.

questions.question: How does Paging avoid External Fragmentation?
questions.answer: By breaking memory into fixed-sized blocks (pages and frames). Any free physical frame can be allocated to any process, eliminating unusable variable-sized gaps.

questions.question: What causes Thrashing and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: Thrashing is caused by lack of physical RAM where the OS spends all time servicing page faults. It is fixed by reducing running processes or installing more RAM.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a Mutex and a Semaphore?
questions.answer: A mutex is an ownership lock (only the locker can unlock). A semaphore is a signaling mechanism with a counter that can be incremented by any thread.

topics.explanation: Memory cards, interview gotcha rules, and structural architecture map for operating systems.
keyPoints: Golden Interview Rules: Process != Thread; Ready != Waiting; Page Fault != Program Crash; Mutex is ownership, Semaphore is signaling.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between User Mode and Kernel Mode?
flashcards.answer: User mode (bit 1) restricts direct hardware access; Kernel mode (bit 0) grants full privileged instruction access.

flashcards.question: What four memory segments make up a process?
flashcards.answer: Text (code), Data (globals), Heap (dynamically allocated memory), and Stack (local variables and functions).

flashcards.question: Ready State vs Waiting State?
flashcards.answer: Ready means waiting purely for CPU time; Waiting means waiting for an external event or I/O completion.

flashcards.question: What is the Convoy Effect?
flashcards.answer: In FCFS scheduling, short processes are delayed for a long time behind a large CPU-bound process.

flashcards.question: How does Aging resolve Starvation in Priority Scheduling?
flashcards.answer: By gradually increasing the priority number of waiting processes the longer they remain in the ready queue.

flashcards.question: What is a Race Condition?
flashcards.answer: A bug where multiple threads modify shared data simultaneously, making final results dependent on execution timing.

flashcards.question: What are the 4 Coffman conditions for Deadlock?
flashcards.answer: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait.

flashcards.question: How do you break the Circular Wait condition?
flashcards.answer: Assign a global numerical ordering to all resources and force processes to acquire locks only in strictly increasing order.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between a Page and a Frame?
flashcards.answer: A Page is a fixed-size block of logical virtual memory; a Frame is an equal fixed-size block of physical RAM.

flashcards.question: What happens during a Page Fault?
flashcards.answer: The CPU traps to the OS, the missing page is located on disk, loaded into a free RAM frame, and the process resumes.

flashcards.question: Internal vs External Fragmentation?
flashcards.answer: External fragmentation leaves free memory scattered in unusable small gaps; Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block.

flashcards.question: What is Thrashing?
flashcards.answer: A state where the OS spends almost 100% of its time swapping pages in and out of disk due to insufficient RAM.

flashcards.question: Vertical Scaling vs Horizontal Scaling?
flashcards.answer: Vertical (Scale Up) upgrades a single server's CPU/RAM; Horizontal (Scale Out) adds more server nodes.

flashcards.question: What does a Load Balancer do?
flashcards.answer: Distributes incoming network traffic evenly across healthy backend worker servers to prevent overloading.

flashcards.question: Reliability vs Availability?
flashcards.answer: Availability is uptime percentage; Reliability is the probability of delivering completely correct service over time.

flashcards.question: What is a Single Point of Failure (SPOF)?
flashcards.answer: Any single architecture component that, if broken, brings down the entire application system.

flashcards.question: What is an API Gateway?
flashcards.answer: A single entry point for clients that routes requests to microservices and handles auth, rate-limiting, and logging.

flashcards.question: What is Amdahl's Law?
flashcards.answer: A law showing that program speedup via multi-core CPUs is strictly limited by the sequential (serial) portion of the code.

flashcards.question: What is Direct Memory Access (DMA)?
flashcards.answer: Hardware that transfers high-speed I/O data blocks directly between memory and devices without burdening the CPU.

flashcards.question: Why is Peterson's Algorithm not reliable on modern multi-core systems?
flashcards.answer: Modern CPUs and compilers reorder read/write instructions for speed, breaking Peterson's strict sequential memory assumptions.

traps.statement: Threads share all memory segments including the stack.
traps.explanation: False. Threads share the code, data, and heap segments, but each thread strictly keeps its own private stack and registers.

traps.statement: A cycle in a resource allocation graph always guarantees a deadlock.
traps.explanation: False. It guarantees deadlock only for single-instance resources. If resources have multiple instances, a cycle might not be deadlocked.
